text: Everything in this chapter leads here: how does a security team actually decide whether a model is robust enough to deploy? Not by running one attack and checking a box. A real evaluation starts before any attack runs at all, with a written threat model, and ends with a report that names exactly what was tested and how.

A threat model has to specify four things: the attacker's goal, whether that's any misclassification or one specific wrong label; their knowledge, white-box access to gradients or black-box query access only; their capability, what perturbation budget and norm is realistic, including whether a problem-space constraint applies; and their access to the deployed model itself. Skip this step, and every number that follows is answering a question nobody actually asked.

The evaluation itself runs through an established library rather than a one-off script — IBM's Adversarial Robustness Toolbox, CleverHans, and Foolbox are the names that show up again and again, each implementing standard attacks like FGSM and PGD consistently. Run the chosen attack against the model at a stated epsilon, measure how often it succeeds, and you have a reproducible number another team could check.

One weak attack surviving is not evidence of robustness. If a defense only holds up against an attack that doesn't know the defense is there, you may just be looking at obfuscated gradients again. A credible evaluation uses PGD as its baseline and, critically, an adaptive attack — one built with the specific defense mechanism in mind, designed to try to defeat exactly that mechanism.

The resulting report has to name its numbers, not just state a verdict: clean accuracy as the baseline, robust accuracy under a named attack at a stated perturbation budget, the attack success rate, and a certified radius if a provable defense like randomized smoothing is in play. And it has to be re-run whenever the model, its data, or its preprocessing changes — a stale robustness number is not a current one.

That closes this chapter. You now have the vocabulary to recognize an adversarial example, the risk category it creates against real classifiers, what the available defenses actually cost, and how to test for all of it before deployment. Chapter six moves from the model itself to the full application built around it.
